title: Code-mixed voice support & collections calls
business_question: A bank, telecom or insurer handling Hinglish/Tanglish/Manglish/Benglish/Kanglish calls: which speech-to-text gets the caller's card digits, amounts, dates and phone numbers right, and which voice-agent stack answers fastest?

dataset.name: uc01 code-mixed customer-care utterances
dataset.how_made: 80 customer-side utterances (16 per code-mix: card block, UPI failure, EMI/collections, telecom recharge/porting, insurance claims) written by hand with a code-mix reference (English in Latin, Indic in native script, numbers as digits), an all-native-script reference, and gold entities. Audio synthesised with macOS `say` Indian voices (Lekha, Vani, Piya, Soumya) and gemini-3.8-flash-tts voices; Sarvam's TTS was not used so the test does not favour Sarvam. Phone condition: 8 kHz 300-3400 Hz band, G.711 mu-law, ~20 dB SNR noise, back to 16 kHz. Phone numbers are arbitrary, not real customers.

metrics.name: WER, best of code-mix / all-native-script reference [clean]
WER, best of code-mix / all-native-script reference [phone]

findings: Entity accuracy (what a bank needs: card last-4, amounts, dates, phone and claim numbers, 100 entities): gemini-3.8-flash 0.94 [0.89-0.98] on both clean and phone-line audio; saaras:v3 codemix 0.74 [0.65-0.83] clean / 0.81 [0.73-0.88] phone; gpt-4o-transcribe 0.61 / 0.57; whisper-1 (hosted Whisper) 0.50 / 0.51; saaras:v3 transcribe 0.43 / 0.46; local whisper-large-v3-turbo 0.24 / 0.26.

saaras:v4 (released 25 Sep 2026) vs v3 on the same clips. Codemix mode: v4 follows the code-mix script convention almost always (1/160 outputs without Latin vs 48/160 for v3) and has lower WER on clean audio (0.27 [0.22-0.33] vs 0.38; phone tie 0.30), but it writes numbers as words far more often, so entity accuracy FALLS: 0.46 clean / 0.39 phone vs v3's 0.74 / 0.81. Numbers-as-words misses per 100 entities: v4 codemix 50 clean / 57 phone vs v3 15 / 11 (e.g. ml: '₹18,000' -> 'പതിനെണ്ണായിരം രൂപ'). Transcribe mode improves: v4 entity accuracy 0.60 / 0.64 vs v3 0.43 / 0.46, numbers-as-words 35 / 31 vs 51 / 52. Best-of-two-references WER: v4 transcribe 0.24 / 0.28 vs v3 0.39 / 0.43. Neither v4 mode reaches gemini-3.8-flash on digits (0.94).

Keyterm prompting (saaras:v4 only; v3 rejects it with HTTP 400) with ONE fixed 50-term list a bank/telecom would configure once — UPI, EMI, KYC, IFSC, NEFT, OTP, PhonePe, Airtel, Jio, postpaid, recharge, claim number, premium… and no per-clip numbers — helps v4 codemix: entity accuracy 0.50 [0.41-0.60] clean / 0.56 [0.47-0.66] phone vs 0.46 / 0.39 without; numbers-as-words misses 45 / 39 vs 50 / 57; WER 0.25 / 0.23 vs 0.27 / 0.30 (phone CER 0.19, the best of any system); occurrences of 14 listed brand/product terms (UPI, EMI, OTP, Airtel, Jio, PhonePe…) written correctly in Latin: 93/106 vs 83/106. A repeat of plain v4 codemix on the phone audio scored 0.38, so the phone gain is not run-to-run noise; the clean gain is within noise. Even with keyterms, v4 codemix stays below v3 codemix (0.74 / 0.81) on digits. Gains are uneven by language: Manglish and Kanglish phone 0.45 -> 0.80 and 0.35 -> 0.70, Benglish unchanged (0.20 -> 0.15). Keyterm calls were slower: p50 1.78 s / p95 6.0 s.

Inverse text normalisation (number words -> digits) was NOT implemented: a parser covering Hindi's 100 irregular number words plus agglutinated Tamil/Malayalam/Kannada/Bengali forms ('நானூற்றி எழுபத்தி ரெண்டு', 'പതിനെണ്ണായിരം') does not fit in ~60 lines. Upper bound instead, same rule for every system (count every miss whose output has no digits at all as recoverable, i.e. assume the spoken-out number is right): phone-line ceiling saaras:v4 codemix 0.96, v4+keyterms 0.95, v4 transcribe 0.95, v3 transcribe 0.98, v3 codemix 0.92, Gemini 0.94, gpt-4o-transcribe 0.71, whisper-1 0.85. So with perfect ITN the Sarvam v4 gap to Gemini could close, but that is a ceiling, not a measured result.
saaras:v4 latency per utterance: p50 0.49-0.51 s (v3 0.61-0.65 s) but a heavier tail, p95 2.8-5.3 s vs ~0.9 s for v3, measured while other agents were rate-limiting the shared account.

Most saaras misses are formatting, not hearing: in codemix mode 15 of 26 clean misses (11 of 19 phone) had no digits at all — the number came back as words (e.g. hi02 'बारह हज़ार चार सौ निन्यानवे', 'सेवन थ्री ज़ीरो सिक्स'). Codemix mode is not applied consistently: 48/160 codemix outputs contain no Latin letters at all, i.e. it fell back to transcribe-style output. Transcribe mode writes numbers as words almost always (51 of 57 misses). Add inverse text normalisation before using saaras output for account data.

Gemini never wrote a number as words (0 such misses); its 6 misses were genuinely wrong digits. It does not follow the script convention reliably either: 59/160 Gemini outputs had no Latin letters (English loanwords written in native script).

Word error rate is convention-bound. Against the code-mix reference, saaras codemix and Gemini tie on clean audio (0.38 vs 0.36) and saaras codemix is better on phone audio (0.30 [0.24-0.36] vs 0.35 [0.31-0.39]); CER on phone audio 0.24 vs 0.37. Scoring each output against whichever reference convention suits it better (code-mix or all-native script, no transliteration), Gemini is lower: 0.17-0.18 vs saaras codemix 0.25.

Phone-line degradation (8 kHz, 300-3400 Hz, mu-law, 20 dB SNR) barely hurt any API system; saaras codemix even scored better on phone than clean, which reflects run-to-run variation in its number formatting rather than a real benefit.

Whisper is not usable for code-mixed Indian calls. Local whisper-large-v3-turbo: WER 0.80 (per-clip capped at 1), entity accuracy 0.24, repetition loops on noisy audio, Malayalam answered in Devanagari on 15 of 32 clips even with language='ml'. Hosted whisper-1 is somewhat better (WER 0.72, entities 0.50) but rejects language='bn' and 'ml' outright (HTTP 400 'Language 'bn' is not supported.'), so Benglish and Manglish ran on auto-detect.

gpt-4o-transcribe (given the same code-mix instruction as Gemini via its prompt field) lands between saaras and Whisper: WER 0.60 / 0.58, best-of-two-references WER 0.35, entity accuracy 0.61 / 0.57. It is strongly voice-sensitive: entity accuracy 0.76 on Gemini-voiced clips but 0.35 on macOS `say` clips, where it often wrote numbers as words ('आठ हजार सात सौ पचास') or dropped digits (reference 417209 -> 47209). Fastest non-Sarvam STT: p50 1.17 s.

Latency per 5-15 s utterance: saaras:v3 p50 0.61 s / p95 0.95 s (RTF ~0.10); gpt-4o-transcribe 1.17 / 1.46 s (RTF 0.19); whisper-1 2.34 / 3.71 s; gemini-3.8-flash 3.9 / 6.8 s (RTF 0.67); local Whisper on a shared, loaded GPU p50 7.9 s.

Voice-agent pipeline (20 turns; time to first audio = STT + full LLM reply + TTS first byte), p50 / p95: Sarvam stack (saaras codemix + sarvam-105b think off + bulbul:v3 stream) 1.48 / 20.5 s; saaras + gpt-5.4-mini + bulbul 2.01 / 2.27 s; OpenAI stack (gpt-4o-transcribe + gpt-5.4-mini + gpt-4o-mini-tts stream) 3.17 / 3.70 s; saaras + claude-haiku-5.5 + bulbul 3.31 / 4.42 s; Gemini stack (gemini STT + gemini-3.8-flash + gemini TTS stream) 6.78 / 23.1 s. LLM p50: sarvam-105b 0.46 s, gpt-5.4-mini 1.12-1.18 s, claude-haiku-5.5 2.40 s, gemini-3.8-flash 2.40 s. TTS first byte p50: bulbul 0.35-0.39 s, gpt-4o-mini-tts 0.81 s, gemini TTS 1.13 s. sarvam-105b's p95 is driven by one 19.5 s reply on a shared account; gpt-5.4-mini was the most consistent.

New Sarvam stack (saaras:v4 codemix -> sarvam-105b -> bulbul:v4-flash HTTP stream): time to first audio p50 1.14 s / p95 5.17 s vs 1.48 / 20.5 s for the v3/bulbul:v3 stack. Stage p50s: STT 0.44 vs 0.57 s, LLM 0.37 vs 0.46 s, TTS first byte 0.31 vs 0.39 s (bulbul:v4-flash p95 0.34 s). Its p95 comes from two saaras:v4 calls of 2.4 and 4.5 s. Replies stayed in the caller's script 18/20 (v3 stack 19/20) and read numbers back correctly 24/30 (v3 25/30); because v4 STT hands the LLM number-words, sarvam-105b sometimes spoke amounts as words or digit-by-digit ('six two four eight'). bulbul:v4-flash rejects the v3 speaker 'shubh' and ships per-language voices (e.g. shubh_hi_customer, gokul_ta_narration, arnab_bn_conversation, chetan_kn_conversation) but none for Malayalam, so Malayalam used the API default voice.

Agent quality, reply in the caller's language and script (>=30% of letters in the caller's script): sarvam-105b 19/20, claude-haiku-5.5 18/20, gemini-3.8-flash 16/20, gpt-5.4-mini 12/20 (OpenAI stack) and 11/20 (on saaras transcripts). gpt-5.4-mini answered Malayalam, Bengali and Kannada callers in Hindi or English 4 times (e.g. 'Sorry for the परेशानी… Aapka ₹560 debit ho gaya' to a Malayalam caller); claude-haiku-5.5 did so once; sarvam-105b never (its one miss was English to a Malayalam caller). Numbers read back correctly: Gemini stack 29/30, Sarvam stack 25/30, OpenAI stack 25/30, saaras+haiku 24/30, saaras+gpt-5.4-mini 23/30 — misheard STT digits propagate ('UPI' -> 'UP', 915 -> 945). claude-haiku-5.5 was the wordiest (~3.9k output tokens over 20 turns vs ~0.7-1.2k for the others), which lengthens TTS.

gemini-3.8-flash with thinking_budget=0 still spent 419-630 thinking tokens on 3 of 20 agent turns (and ~290 on others in a discarded first run, where a 300-token cap truncated replies mid-sentence); the final run used a 1000-token cap. 'Think off' is not a hard switch on this model.

Cost per conversation-minute (caller + agent audio), all-Sarvam stack at list prices: saaras STT Rs 0.23 + sarvam-105b Rs 0.015 + bulbul TTS Rs 1.32 (441 chars/min at Rs 30 per 10k chars) = Rs 1.56; TTS is 85% of it. Swapping the LLM for gpt-5.4-mini or claude-haiku-5.5 raises bulbul's share because those replies are longer (Rs 1.52 and Rs 1.81 per minute for TTS alone); claude-haiku-5.5 via OpenRouter cost USD 0.0022 for all 20 turns as reported. Gemini and OpenAI usage is recorded per conversation-minute in agent_pipeline (tokens/characters; not priced here). The v4 stack comes to Rs 1.42 per minute assuming v3 list prices for saaras:v4 and bulbul:v4-flash (no v4 price given to us).

Sarvam API behaviour under a shared account (other agents active): one window returned HTTP 402 'No credits available' for every call, and STT/TTS/LLM calls hit 429 'Rate limit exceeded'. 87 STT calls ended as HTTP 400 'Failed to read the file' — these were our harness's fault, not Sarvam's: common/bench.py sarvam_post retries a 429 by re-sending the same, already-read file handle, i.e. an empty upload. Re-opening the file per attempt fixed it. Production clients need backoff on 429 and must rebuild multipart bodies on retry.
caveats: Audio is synthetic (macOS `say` Indian voices for Hindi/Tamil/Bengali/Kannada, gemini-3.8-flash-tts for the rest and all Malayalam). TTS speech is cleaner and more regular than real callers; absolute error rates on real calls will be higher.

Possible home advantage for Gemini on Gemini-voiced audio: on the 64 non-Malayalam clips per source, Gemini entity accuracy is 0.92 on `say` audio vs 0.97 on Gemini audio, but saaras codemix also improves (0.68 -> 0.81), so Gemini's lead holds on audio it did not generate.

Gemini TTS read a style instruction aloud in 38 of 48 clips in the first synthesis pass; those clips were regenerated from the bare text and every STT result on them re-run. No clip was hand-checked by listening.
References were written by one author; spellings of English loanwords in native script vary (யுபிஐ/யூபிஐ), which inflates every system's WER. That is why entity accuracy, not WER, is the headline.

Entity matching joins digit groups and ignores separators but does not convert number words to digits. A deployment with an inverse-text-normalisation step would recover many saaras misses; the score measures raw API output.
80 utterances, 100 entities per condition: CIs are roughly +/-0.05 to +/-0.09. Per-language numbers rest on 16 utterances each and are indicative only.

Agent latency was measured from a Mac in India over the public internet on one afternoon, on a shared Sarvam account under load from other jobs; LLM replies were not streamed (full response time), TTS was streamed (time to first byte).
verdict: For capturing what a collections or card-services call actually needs — the digits — use gemini-3.8-flash as the transcriber or add a number-normalisation step after Sarvam: Gemini got 94% of amounts, card digits, dates and phone numbers exactly; saaras:v3 codemix 74-81%; the newer saaras:v4 codemix only 39-46% because it spells numbers out as words (v4 transcribe 60-64%); gpt-4o-transcribe ~60%; hosted whisper-1 ~50%. If you adopt saaras:v4 for its cleaner code-mix text (lower WER, consistent Latin for English words), configure a keyterm list (it lifted phone-line entity accuracy from 0.39 to 0.56 and gave the lowest phone CER of any system) and still budget an inverse-text-normalisation step — without it, v4 is a regression for numeric data versus v3. For the full voice loop, Sarvam's stack is the fastest available: the v4 stack (saaras:v4 + sarvam-105b + bulbul:v4-flash) starts speaking in ~1.1 s p50 (v3 stack 1.5 s, OpenAI 3.2 s, Gemini 6.8 s), and sarvam-105b is the fastest reply LLM and the most reliable at answering in the caller's language. Do not use Whisper (local or hosted) for code-mixed Indian calls.
